Mechanism study · GRDM · Berka · leakage-free split

Where the Signal Dies

GRDM synthetic Berka data loses three-quarters of its downstream predictive signal. Five experiments locate the loss precisely: it is not that synthetic data encodes different relationships, but that the relationships are absent — and the absence is confined to features that cross a table boundary.

Task 01

Can synthetic rows stand in for real ones?

No. Holding training size fixed and swapping real rows for synthetic buys at most +0.01 AUROC over simply dropping those rows — and on loan default it is negative at every ratio.

Total training rows held fixed at the real training size; only composition changes. This is substitution, not augmentation. The comparison that carries the weight is against a control that keeps the same real fraction and drops the rest.

Tasks 02 & 03

Do synthetic-learned rules transfer to the real database?

They barely exist to transfer. Synthetic→real keeps 29% (card) / 20% (loan) of the real model’s above-chance AUROC — but synthetic→synthetic is no better, which reframes the whole failure.

The synthetic database is cut into train and test with the same account-level, outcome-stratified protocol used for the real split, so a synthetic test set is a genuinely held-out relational database rather than a slice of a feature matrix. Training rows are matched across all four cells, so no cell wins on quantity.

Balanced accuracy is at chance in every cell except real→real (card 0.681, loan 0.568); macro-F1 likewise. Loan’s synthetic test set holds only 10 positives, so its tested-on-synthetic column is noise — read the tested-on-real column.

Why this rules out “different relationships”

If synthetic data had learned different but internally consistent rules, the synthetic→synthetic cell would be high and synthetic→real low. It is not. And on card, a real-trained model scores 0.596 on synthetic rows while a synthetic-trained one scores 0.594 — a model that demonstrably knows the real rule does no better on synthetic data than one trained on synthetic noise. Both readings agree: the structure is missing, not different.

Task 04

Which features lose their meaning?

Exactly the ones that cross a table boundary. Own-row and 1-hop features keep 60–81% of their predictive signal; rollups over a sibling table keep 14–21%.

Each feature’s univariate AUROC against the label, measured inside each database. No model is involved, so this separates “the generator did not reproduce this relationship” from “the classifier chose not to use it”.

The number that closes the loop

disp_type — a direct parent–child link — keeps 102% of its signal (real 0.595 → synth 0.597, KS 0.005) and is the synthetic model’s top feature by gain (0.233 vs the real model’s 0.215). On its own it is worth 0.595 AUROC, which is effectively the entire synthetic→synthetic score of 0.594 and close to synthetic→real 0.608. The synthetic-trained card model is, to a first approximation, that one surviving feature.

Meanwhile the real model’s power source trans_balance_mean — worth 0.838 AUROC alone — collapses to 0.511. On loan the two models’ importance rankings are anti-correlated: Spearman ρ = −0.138, top-10 overlap 2/10 (card: ρ = 0.208, 5/10).

Task 05

Is the collapse specific, or is everything degraded?

Specific. For the collapsed aggregates the synthetic AUROC’s 95% CI covers 0.5 in all three seeds — the relationship is not weakened, it is statistically absent. For the matched controls it excludes 0.5 in all three.

Bootstrap CIs on every AUROC and per-seed values rather than a pooled number, with a control group drawn from the same task so “aggregates collapsed” can be told apart from “the generator broke everything”.

Cross-cutting

One seed would have told a different story — on loan only

Seed 0 looks like a partial success on every loan measurement in this study. Seeds 1 and 2 do not. The same fragility does not appear on card ownership anywhere.

What a single loan seed would have produced

Had this study run seed 0 only, we would have reported synthetic→real loan transfer at 0.629 — 44% of the real model’s above-chance AUROC, roughly double the true 3-seed figure of 19.7% — and concluded that loan-default dependencies partially survive. They do not.

Card ownership shows no such fragility: its widest cross-domain cell range is 0.020, and every aggregate is dead in all three seeds. The conclusions of this study rest on card; loan corroborates in direction, not in magnitude.

Reading

What this changes

  • The failure has an address. GRDM reproduces per-table marginals and direct parent–child links, and destroys aggregate dependencies that cross the parent to a sibling table. That is a structural property, not a tuning problem.
  • “Biased” and “shifted” are the wrong words. There is no alternative relationship in the synthetic data to correct for. There is an absence. Any mitigation framed as re-weighting or domain adaptation is aimed at a problem that is not there.
  • There is now a model-free target. The univariate AUROC of a child-aggregate feature, measured inside the generated database, should match its real counterpart. Today it retains 11–13%. Unlike a column-shape score, this cannot be satisfied by getting the marginals right — trans_balance_last has an almost perfect marginal and zero signal.
  • Fidelity metrics remain the wrong gate. These same generators score 96.9 Column Shapes and 91.4 1-Hop. Nothing in this study is visible from those numbers.
Limits, stated plainly

Card’s control group is imperfect. year (0.611 → 0.520) and frequency also degrade, so the card contrast is 10.7% vs 40.9%, not a clean 10% vs 100%. Loan’s control is the clean one at 99.4%.

Fan-out count is not what carries card signal. trans_n (real AUROC 0.534) and order_n (0.512) barely separate the classes — on card it is the balance rollups that matter. Earlier work emphasised counts based on the loan task; both are child aggregates, but they are not interchangeable.

Loan’s conventional aggregates sit at chance in real data (0.43–0.49) because its transaction rollups are cut off at trans_date < loan_date. The loan arm here uses the code-share rollups that actually carry signal.

Method

How to reproduce

  • Generator berka_split, trained on split_train only — no test rows were ever seen.
  • Identical feature builders, untuned XGBoost hyperparameters and metric code across every cell, reused unchanged from the existing harness so these numbers are comparable to prior runs.
  • The synthetic database is split with splits.berka_account_split — account-level, outcome-stratified, 25%, seed 0 — the same call that produced the real split.
  • Training row counts matched within each GRDM seed. Reported ± is the standard deviation across all 15 repeats.
  • Bootstrap CIs: 400 resamples of the evaluated rows, percentile method.
python -m downstream.ratio_report                             # Task 1
python -m downstream.crossdomain --dataset berka_split        # Tasks 2-3
python -m downstream.crossdomain_report
python -m downstream.feature_compare --dataset berka_split    # Task 4
python -m downstream.feature_provenance
python -m downstream.aggregate_validation                     # Task 5
